t3hu-sb-strategy: The HU SB: The Only Player Who Closes Every Street

In full ring the SB is the worst seat: second-to-last preflop, permanently OOP postflop, forced to post a blind with almost no postflop advantage. The HU SB is completely different — you are the button, and your posted 0.5 also acts as an ante: whether or not you eventually participate, that 0.5 has entered the pot as dead money. These two structural facts make the HU SB the seat that must commit first preflop yet holds all the postflop information: preflop you act before seeing the BB's decision; postflop the BB moves first on every street and you decide last. Understanding this dual identity is the starting point of all strategies in this chapter. (Concepts from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.3 preflop strategy; Easy Game, Andrew Seidman Ch.4 position)

The SB's 0.5 in heads-up is a "forced ante": it isn't an avoidable sunk cost but part of the prize pool you and the BB contest. You close every postflop street — the treatment the full-ring SB dreams of — at the price of committing first preflop (the position reversal, detailed in this level's “Position Reversal” chapter).
Opening Size: Min-Raise Is the Main Weapon

The math of an SB min-raise to 2BB (SB already posted 0.5, extra risk 1.5BB; BB posted 1, can fold or complete 1):

Pure blind-steal model (baseline = SB folds immediately; the 0.5 dead money is sunk): SB extra risk 1.5BB, and if BB folds the SB wins the whole 1.5BB pot
EV(raise) = f×1.5 − (1−f)×1.5 (f = BB fold rate)
Break-even: f×1.5 = (1−f)×1.5 → f = 50%
So if the BB folds more than 50%, the pure blind-steal part of the SB's min-raise with any two cards starts to profit;
equivalently, the BB's minimum defense frequency MDF = 1 − 50% = 50%.

Opening sizes compared (SB extra risk → break-even fold rate):
min-raise 2BB: 1.5BB → 1.5÷3 = 50%
2.5BB: 2BB → 2÷3.5 ≈ 57.1%
3BB: 2.5BB → 2.5÷4 = 62.5%

Conclusion: the smaller the size, the lower the automatic-profit bar; in heads-up the BB actually defends 60%-70%+ (folding only 30%-40%), so the min-raise's pure blind-steal part is negative — the real profit is postflop. (Concepts from: Applications of No-Limit Hold'em, Matthew Janda Ch.3 blind games; Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.3 preflop strategy)

Why min-raise dominates HU opening? Three points: (1) low steal bar — 2BB needs only 50% fold rate, while the real HU BB fold rate vs min-raise is only about 30%-40%, so pure blind-stealing barely profits; the open's value is postflop, and the smaller the size the easier postflop pot control; (2) big sizes in heads-up are "self-punishment" — the BB's calling range narrows with size, so spending 3BB only buys a stronger calling range; and although you hold postflop position, running a wide range into a big pot costs far more than in full ring; (3) frequency and balance — min-raise lets you open about 80% of hands, and only a wide enough range covers various flops. The full-ring wisdom "steal blinds with bigger sizes" must be reversed in heads-up: sizing serves postflop, not the steal.

The HU SB limp is an exception to full-ring dogma. In full ring the SB almost never limps, because after a limp, facing a multiway raise loses position, enters passively, and gives up fold equity; but in heads-up three reasons make limping a GTO-reasonable option: (1) odds — completing 0.5 to see a 1.5 pot needs only 25% required equity, and any hand against the BB's wide range is close to or above that line; (2) structure — the BB has the final say preflop, so after a limp he can only check or raise (isolate), and your postflop button comes from the rules themselves — limping costs you no extra position; (3) range protection — mixing AA/KK into the limp range stops the BB from mindlessly isolating limps. Solvers show the HU SB limps about 20%-30% of the time (adjusting by stack depth and opponent), with min-raise the rest. (Concepts from: Modern Poker Theory, Michael Acevedo Ch.3 preflop play and limp mixing; Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.3 preflop strategy)

Example: HU 100BB deep, you (SB) hold A♠5♠. First tier the hand: strong made hands (JJ+, AK) go into the raise pile for both value and steal; speculative hands (small pairs, suited connectors, A5s-like) mix between the limp and raise piles; junk (K8o, Q6o) folds. A5s's home depends on the BB's 3-bet frequency: at a 15% BB 3-bet, A5s gets 3-bet about 15% of the time and usually must fold — the min-raise EV erodes about 0.15×1.5 ≈ 0.23BB, making the limp pile cheaper; below an 8% 3-bet, A5s's blocker value (fewer AA/AK for the opponent) and postflop nut-draw potential make min-raise the better choice. The same hand's home is decided by the opponent's 3-bet frequency — the first practical taste of "ranges move with the opponent".

Example 2: You (SB) hold 7♥6♥, 100BB deep. Against a calling station (almost never folds postflop): min-raise steal EV = 0.35×1.5 − 0.65×1.5 ≈ −0.45BB (pure-steal basis), while after a limp 76s has about 43% equity vs the BB's random range, and deep-stacked your made straights/flushes get paid in full — limping into the flop (or even folding marginal hands) is clearly better than raising. Different opponent: BB is a nit (folds about 70%), min-raise steal EV = 0.7×1.5 − 0.3×1.5 = +0.6BB, and 76s is worth raising too. The same 76s: limp against a station, raise against a nit — the HU SB's sizes and actions aren't fixed but respond directly to the BB's defense frequency.

Counterintuitive point: "limping is weak and always wrong" is full-ring dogma; transplanting it into heads-up bleeds EV continuously. The HU SB limp has GTO backing: dead-money odds of 25%, an untouched postflop button, and range protection combined. The real error isn't limping itself but "a limp range with no strong hands" — that's what gets mindlessly isolated.

SB opening three-pile quick memory: raise pile (JJ+, AK, A5s-type blockers), limp pile (small/medium pairs, suited connectors, weak suited Ax), fold pile (junk below K8o). Every 50 hands check: does your limp pile have enough strong hands mixed in? Is the BB's 3-bet driving you out of the raise pile? Both answers decide the next round's frequency adjustments.
t3hu-bb-defense: BB: The Most Profitable Seat in Heads-Up

The full-ring BB is a long-term losing seat: acting last preflop is the only comfort, and being permanently OOP postflop makes 85%-92% equity realization the norm. The HU BB keeps the final say preflop, and the 1BB it already posted is dead money that makes any call cheap; but postflop the BB speaks first while the SB has the last word as the button. So the HU BB profits from price and range width, not from postflop position: having the final preflop say buys no postflop position, and because the BB moves first on every street he needs the check-raise lever and a wider defense to compensate. (Concepts from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.2 position and equity; Easy Game, Andrew Seidman Ch.4 position)

BB's defense floor vs an SB 3BB open (MDF):

Perspective 1 (dead-money): SB's total 3BB is the risk, both blinds 1.5BB the prize
SB automatic-profit fold rate f* = 3 ÷ (1.5+3) = 3 ÷ 4.5 ≈ 66.7%
BB minimum defense frequency MDF = 1 − 66.7% ≈ 33.3%

Perspective 2 (raise amount): SB's raise amount 2.5BB, pre-bet pot 1.5BB
MDF = 1 − 2.5 ÷ (1.5+2.5) = 1 − 2.5 ÷ 4 = 37.5%

Both perspectives give the same conclusion: BB's defense floor is about 33%-38% — below this the SB auto-profits opening any two cards. (Concepts from: Applications of No-Limit Hold'em, Matthew Janda Ch.3 blind games and MDF; Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.3 preflop odds calculation)

But MDF is only the floor that "stops auto-profit", not the optimal defense frequency. Solvers show the HU BB actually defends about 60%-70% against an SB open (calls ~35%-50% + 3-bets ~15%-25%), far above the 33%-38% floor, for three reasons: (1) dead money — the SB's 0.5 makes calls cheap: vs a min-raise the BB only needs 1BB more, required equity = call ÷ (current pot + opponent's bet + your call) = 1 ÷ (1.5 + 1.5 + 1) = 1 ÷ 4 = 25% (the current pot of 1.5 already contains the BB's own 1BB — dead money, yes, but still in the denominator, never drop it); the same result follows from t2hu's EV(call) = E×(P+B) − (1−E)×B with P = the opponent's total investment 2BB and B = your call 1BB: setting EV=0 gives E = B ÷ (P + 2B) = 1 ÷ (2 + 2) = 25%; (2) the SB's range is wide and weak — the HU SB opens about 80% of hands, so the BB's weak hands clear the 25% call line comfortably; (3) the MDF model scores "continue" as zero EV, but whenever the BB realizes part of his equity through his first-acting levers (check-raise and check-call), the call turns +EV. The cost is written into the structure too: postflop the BB is the out-of-position side, so his equity realizes at a discount and his defense must be wider than full ring to pay. MDF answers "how little must I defend"; dead money and the opponent's range answer "how much more can I defend" — the HU BB's 60%+ is the sum of the two.

The HU BB's "60%+ defense" is defense bought by price: you hold the final preflop say and your posted blind is already dead money, so calling with marginal hands costs far less than in full ring. Transplanting the full-ring intuition "BB must play tight" into heads-up is throwing away that cheap calling line.
Call vs 3-bet: The Two Legs of Defense

Against an SB open, the BB's defense range splits into two piles. The call pile: small/medium pairs (22-TT), suited connectors (65s+), weak suited Aces (A2s-A9s), weak suited Kings (K6s-K9s) — these realize equity through the cheap price and implied odds, winning without showdown. The 3-bet pile has two layers: value (JJ+, AK — clearly ahead of the SB's wide range, and also compress the SB's steal frequency) and bluff (blocker-bearing combos like A5s, A4s, K8s — blocking AA/KK/AK, making the SB harder to 4Bet). Facing a 3-bet the SB either 4Bets or folds, so the bluff layer must pick hands that "can fold cleanly to a 4Bet". The Gap Concept corrected for the HU BB: full ring requires stronger hands to call a raise (the gap), but the HU BB has already posted 1BB dead money, so his call price is tiny and he can push well past the gap — this is the source of the 60%+ BB defense vs the 25%-50% full-ring BB defense. (Concepts from: The Theory of Poker, David Sklansky Ch.2-3 Gap Concept; Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.3 preflop strategy)

Example: HU 100BB deep, SB min-raises to 2BB, you (BB) hold K♠7♠. K7s is a typical marginal hand in solver BB calling ranges: calling 1BB makes the total pot SB 2 + the BB's own 1 + your call 1 = 4BB, required equity = 1 ÷ 4 = 25% (general formula: call ÷ (current pot 1.5 + opponent's bet 1.5 + your call 1)); K7s vs the SB's ~80% open range wins about 48% — about 23 points of surplus. Postflop you act first (OOP): a K flop lets you lead thin value, flush/straight draws chase cheaply, and a complete miss can fold. Folding gives up 48% equity that can be contested at 25% odds — the most typical HU BB error: importing the full-ring memory "K7s is a bad hand". Facing a full-ring UTG open K7s is indeed a fold, but vs the HU SB's 80% range it's a +EV call.

Example 2 (isolate): SB limps (completes 0.5), you (BB) hold A♠8♠, 100BB deep, and the SB folds to a raise about 55%. Isolate-raise to 4BB: EV ≈ 0.55×1.5 (win dead money on a fold) + 0.45×(+0.5) (initiative and range advantage about +0.5BB when called) ≈ +1.05BB; while checking is only about +0.7BB (small pot, letting the SB realize a weak range for free). Isolating earns about 0.35BB more than checking. But note: isolating isn't blind-stealing — the SB's limp already exposed a weak range, and your raise is "punishing the weak range + seizing initiative"; when called, A8s's showdown value leaves you comfortable postflop. The higher the opponent's limp-fold frequency, the higher your isolate frequency should be.

Counterintuitive point: BB defending 60%+ isn't "calling station". A real station has no 3-bet pile and no isolating raises — while the HU BB's 60% consists of calls, 3-bet value, and 3-bet bluffs, each moving with the SB's tendencies. Defense width and defense passivity are two different things.

BB defense three-step quick check: (1) call the pot odds — calling line 25% vs a 2BB open (1BB more into a 4BB total pot), 33.3% vs a 3BB open (2BB more into a 6BB total pot); (2) split piles — cheap-price call pile, strong-made 3-bet value, blocker-bluff 3-bet; (3) watch the SB — raise 3-bet frequency vs an over-folder, raise isolate frequency vs a big limper, narrow the call pile vs a frequent 3-better. After three steps, 60% defense is structured choice rather than "reluctant to fold".
t3hu-position-reversal: Position Reversal: The Unique Identity Swap in Heads-Up

Full-ring position is "assigned": the BTN acts last every hand, the SB/BB are OOP every hand, and positional attributes never change. Heads-up position "reverses": the BB has the final say preflop but must move first postflop (losing position); the SB is the opposite — he commits first preflop yet closes every street as the button. Every hand, the one who got the preflop advantage pays it back postflop, and the one passive preflop collects rent postflop. This reversal is heads-up's most overlooked structural fact: full-ring players new to HU often play postflop with the full-ring mentality "I'm the aggressor, I have initiative", and get repeatedly harvested by the SB's positional advantage. (Concepts from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.2 position theory; Easy Game, Andrew Seidman Ch.4 position)

The cruel face of the reversal: the BB's final preflop say can't buy postflop position. Preflop you commit last; postflop you move first — "initiative" belongs to you only until the flop; once the flop comes, every SB decision comes after yours.

Street-by-street positional-value model (limp pot starting 2BB, half-pot bet + call each street):

Pot sequence: flop 2BB → turn 4BB → river 8BB
Per-street bet: flop 1BB → turn 2BB → river 4BB

Assume position gives a "5% decision advantage per street" (information + pot control folded in):
Flop contribution: 1BB × 5% = 0.05BB
Turn contribution: 2BB × 5% = 0.10BB
River contribution: 4BB × 5% = 0.20BB
Total positional value ≈ 0.35BB/hand, with the river at 0.20 ÷ 0.35 ≈ 57%

Conclusion: more than half of positional value is realized on the river — "river position matters most" isn't a slogan but the mathematical necessity of geometric pot growth. Note: T2's 0.5-1BB/hand positional value estimates the total including preflop positional advantage; this section's 0.35BB quantifies only the postflop part under conservative assumptions, a component of the former. (Concepts from: Heads-Up No-Limit Hold'em, Collin Moshman Ch.2 position and equity; Harrington on Hold'em, Dan Harrington Vol.1 Ch.5 position and equity)

Why is river positional value greatest? Three mechanisms: (1) biggest pot — the same 5% decision advantage operates on an 8BB pot, 4× the chip magnitude of the flop; (2) narrowest range, most complete information — after two rounds of flop/turn filtering both ranges have narrowed greatly, and the last actor makes the final ruling on the most precise read; (3) irreversible decision — the river is the last street: IP can "bet, fold to a raise", while OOP suffers the dilemma of "checked and stolen from, or bet and raised". The same button mechanics apply here: in heads-up the BTN is the SB, every single hand — the quantitative explanation for why the HU SB realizes more of its equity postflop.

Example: HU 100BB deep, SB min-raises to 2BB, BB calls with A♠Q♠, pot 4BB. Flop K♥8♦3♣. The first frame of the reversal: the BB had the final preflop say but now must move first — the SB holds the position. BB checks, the SB bets 2BB (half pot, pot to 6BB); you call, pot 8BB, you've invested 2BB, required equity 25%. Your AQ equity: Kx density in the SB's betting range on this king-high board runs about 30% (an instructional anchor; measuring the SB's ~80% opening range as a whole lands nearer 20%, which only lifts the weighted figure to about 23%); without a K, AQ has about 27% via 6 overcard outs plus a backdoor flush, with a K only about 6% — weighted ≈ 0.7×27% + 0.3×6% ≈ 21%, and both readings (21%-23%) sit under the 25% call line, so the standard answer is fold. The same A♠Q♠ from the SB's seat: after the BB checks he can bet half pot to take the pot or check behind for a free turn; AQ goes from "a fold at the call-line edge" to "a vehicle of initiative". The reversal makes the same hand worth nearly a full pot difference between the two seats.

OOP compensates for the reversal with three tools: (1) check as the default — the OOP default is handing the decision to IP, hiding hand strength with the "checking range", and if the SB checks behind you see a free card; (2) check-raise (x/r) — about 10%-15% of OOP decisions choose x/r, with a range of nuts/very strong hands + suitable bluffs (strong draws, blockers), whose purpose is suppressing IP's betting frequency and protecting the check-call range from exploitation; (3) donk bet — OOP leads out, rare in solvers (about 2%-5% of board structures), because the donk range is naturally strong, can't balance when raised, and gives up the x/r lever; exceptions occur on specific boards where OOP's range dominates (e.g. after an SB limp on 6♠5♦4♣ with high two-pair/straight density), where donking to protect equity is actually optimal. Remember: donk is the exception, not the norm — full-ring beginners love to donk to "protect their hand", and in heads-up it's a free advertisement of range imbalance. (Concepts from: Modern Poker Theory, Michael Acevedo Ch.4 postflop play and OOP structure; Harrington on Hold'em, Dan Harrington Vol.1 Ch.5 position and equity)

Example 2 (river positional value): HU blinds 0.5/1, preflop SB min-raises 2BB, BB calls, pot 4BB. Flop Q♠8♦3♣, BB checks, SB bets 2BB, pot 8BB. Turn 2♥, BB checks, SB bets 4BB, pot 16BB. River 9♠, both players hold a Q with a K kicker (e.g. you hold K♦Q♦, the opponent K♥Q♥ — top pair Q + K kicker). Scenario A — you're in the SB (in position): the BB checks, you bet about 5BB (1/3 pot) for thin value, and can safely fold to a raise (88/33/99 in the BB's range all raise reasonably), netting about 5BB; Scenario B — you're in the BB (out of position): you check, the SB bets 8BB, and your top pair degrades into a "call to catch bluffs or fold" choice; if you lead 8BB, top pair Q is hard to fold when raised in a 100BB-deep game. Same hand, same betting line — IP realizes 5BB of thin value while OOP can only respond passively. The river's 57% positional-value share becomes real money here.

Counterintuitive point: even the preflop aggressor, though holding position, cannot bet every street. The SB's continuation-bet frequency is far below the full-ring BTN's — because the BB defends a very wide range, so the SB's own wide range gets "diluted" postflop, and the side that acts first can always answer with a check-raise. The right use of initiative is as "narrative rights", not "the right to bet": an OOP check isn't weakness but kicking the ball to IP and deciding whether to accept.

OOP decision-flow four questions: how big is the pot (does SPR call for pot control)? How often will IP bet after my check (decides check-call vs x/r)? Do I have nuts in my range (decides x/r frequency)? Does my range dominate this board (decides whether to donk)? After four questions, the reversed position goes from passive suffering to structured game.

t3hu-sb-strategy-q1.question: The SB's 0.5 blind in heads-up is described as "also acting as an ante". The most accurate understanding is:
options: It's invested dead money that stays in the prize pool whether or not the SB participates, giving limp and steal their mathematical basis
It's automatically returned to the SB at the end of preflop
It only applies when the BB also limps
It lets the SB see the flop for free without further investment
t3hu-sb-strategy-q1.explanation: The SB's 0.5 enters the pot whether or not he participates, with ante-like dead-money properties: limping completes 0.5 to see a 1.5 pot (25% required equity), and stealing contests it as a prize. Option B contradicts the rules, C confuses the ante's condition, and D ignores that the SB still completes the blind difference.

t3hu-sb-strategy-q2.question: SB min-raises to 2BB; assuming the EV when called or 3-bet is zero, at what BB fold rate does the SB auto-profit with any two cards?
options: About 40%
About 50%
About 60%
About 75%
t3hu-sb-strategy-q2.explanation: Baseline = SB folds immediately (the 0.5 is sunk): f×1.5 = (1−f)×1.5 → f = 50% break-even. GTO BBs actually fold only about 30%-40%, so pure stealing is negative — the value of opening is postflop. 40%/60%/75% don't match the derivation.

t3hu-sb-strategy-q3.question: Why is the SB limp a GTO-reasonable option in heads-up but almost never in full ring?
options: The 0.5 completion price needs only 25% equity, and a limp never costs the SB the postflop button — after a limp the BB can only check or raise
HU pots are smaller, so limping's loss is negligible
After a limp the BB cannot raise, so the SB sees the flop for free
Full-ring rules forbid the SB from limping
t3hu-sb-strategy-q3.explanation: The core is structural: the HU SB has posted 0.5 dead money (completing 0.5 contests a 1.5 pot at 25% odds) and a limp never changes the postflop button he already holds; the full-ring SB is the second-to-last preflop actor, and after a limp a multiway raise costs him both position and initiative. Claiming the BB cannot raise after a limp ignores the rules, and the rest contradict the odds structure or full-ring play.

t3hu-sb-strategy-q4.question: The BB isolates your limp at 70% frequency; you (SB) hold K♠8♠ deep. The optimal adjustment is:
options: Keep limping normally and rely on postflop
Drastically reduce limping — switch marginal hands to min-raise or direct fold, leaving only strong hands in the limp pile
Increase limping to fight back with more hands
Switch to 4x opening sizes
t3hu-sb-strategy-q4.explanation: A 70% isolate frequency means your limp almost always gets attacked: the 25%-odds plan to see a flop fails, and marginal hands must either fold or continue weak into a 3-bet pot. The correct adjustment is narrowing the limp pile and using min-raise to reclaim initiative; continuing to limp is being exploited, limping more amplifies the leak, and 4x sizes only make the BB fold weak hands and keep strong ones.

t3hu-bb-defense-q1.question: The typical HU BB defense frequency vs an SB open is about:
t3hu-bb-defense-q1.explanation: Solvers show the HU BB defends about 60%-70% (calls 35%-50% + 3-bets 15%-25%). 15%-25% is the full-ring vs a tight open magnitude, and 85%-95% is a passive calling station's magnitude — neither is GTO.

t3hu-bb-defense-q2.question: SB opens 3BB (total 3). By the dead-money perspective, the BB's minimum defense frequency (MDF) is about:
options: About 20%
About 33%
About 50%
About 67%
t3hu-bb-defense-q2.explanation: MDF = 1 − 3/(1.5+3) = 1 − 66.7% ≈ 33.3%. 67% is the BB fold rate the SB needs to auto-profit (f*); 20% and 50% don't match the derivation. Note MDF is only the floor; GTO actually defends 60%-70%, far above it.

t3hu-bb-defense-q3.question: Why is the GTO HU BB defense frequency (60%-70%) far above the MDF floor (33%-38%)?
options: Because the BB's cards are better than the SB's
Because the SB's dead money makes the BB's call price tiny and his equity vs a wide range clears it, so calling is +EV
Because the MDF formula doesn't apply preflop
Because the BB must stop the SB from stealing with any cards
t3hu-bb-defense-q3.explanation: MDF only guarantees "stopping pure-bluff auto-profit"; the BB's call +EV comes from the SB's 0.5 dead money, the SB's wide range, and the equity the BB realizes with his first-acting check-raise lever — allowing defense above the floor while still profiting. The missing postflop position is the price he pays, which is why the defense must be wide. The remaining choices conflict with dealing randomness, MDF's scope, or the floor/optimum distinction.

t3hu-bb-defense-q4.question: After an SB limp, you (BB) hold A♠8♠ and the SB folds to a raise about 55%. The optimal action is:
options: Check, letting the flop come free
Isolate-raise to about 4BB
Raise to 10BB for maximum pressure
Fold directly
t3hu-bb-defense-q4.explanation: Isolate EV ≈ 0.55×1.5 + 0.45×0.5 ≈ +1.05BB, clearly above checking's ~+0.7BB. Raising to 10BB over-pressures — the SB only continues with strong hands and your A8s's postflop equity crashes; checking lets the SB realize a weak range for free; folding wastes the showdown value bought at that cheap price.

t3hu-position-reversal-q1.question: The most accurate meaning of "position reversal" in heads-up is:
options: The BB has the final preflop say but moves first postflop; the SB must commit first preflop but closes every street
The SB and BB swap the button every hand
The BB bets first after the flop
Positional advantage disappears on the river
t3hu-position-reversal-q1.explanation: Heads-up: the BB has the final preflop say and moves first postflop (no postflop position); the SB is the opposite — heads-up's unique position reversal. The remaining choices misread the button rule, name the wrong side as the first postflop actor, or contradict "river position matters most".

t3hu-position-reversal-q2.question: In the street-by-street positional model (flop/turn/river contributions 0.05/0.10/0.20BB), the river accounts for about what share of total positional value?
options: About 33%
About 43%
About 57%
About 67%
t3hu-position-reversal-q2.explanation: Total value = 0.05 + 0.10 + 0.20 = 0.35BB; river share = 0.20/0.35 ≈ 57%. 33% is the three-street average (1/3); 67% wrongly compares the river against the flop alone.

t3hu-position-reversal-q3.question: Why does postflop OOP usually avoid donk betting?
options: Donk betting is prohibited by the rules
The donk range is naturally strong, can't balance when raised, and gives up the check-raise lever
OOP should always check-call
Donk betting only works in small pots
t3hu-position-reversal-q3.explanation: A donk range is strong-heavy and can't balance when IP raises; it also forfeits the x/r lever, freely exposing range strength. It only appears as an exception on boards where OOP's range dominates (e.g. high two-pair/straight density in limp pots). A contradicts the rules, C is too absolute (OOP has the x/r lever), and D has no basis.

t3hu-position-reversal-q4.question: You (BB) call an SB min-raise with K♠Q♠ on a K♦9♣3♠ flop; the SB (in position) is an aggressive high-float player. The optimal tendency is:
options: Bet 2/3 pot immediately to take it down
Mix checks with small (about 1/3 pot) lead bets, keeping the check-raise lever and pot control
Check 100%, always yielding initiative
Shove directly to protect top pair
t3hu-position-reversal-q4.explanation: OOP vs a float-happy player, big bets are extremely costly (you must fold to a raise), shoving is overkill, and 100% checking makes your range transparent and exploitable. Mixing checks with small lead bets: small bets make marginal hands pay to see cards, checks keep the x/r lever, and the frequency balance keeps IP from pinning down your top-pair strength — the combined application of OOP compensation tools.

t3hu-sb-strategy: Understand the HU SB's structural uniqueness — holding the button and closing every postflop street, plus the 0.5 forced ante dead money, opposite to the full-ring SB
Master the math of SB opening sizes: break-even fold rate and MDF, understanding why min-raise is the HU main weapon
Learn to split the limp and raise piles, understanding the GTO rationale for HU limping and its opponent-dependent adjustment conditions
t3hu-bb-defense: Understand how the HU BB's price advantage turns a full-ring losing seat into a profitable one, and what compensation the missing postflop position requires
